newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Poles, Czechs agree joint help on NATO, EU efforts.
newsitem.headline: Poles, Czechs agree joint help on NATO, EU efforts.

text.p: Poland and the Czech Republic, widely seen as frontrunners among former East Bloc countries seeking to join the European Union and NATO, agreed on Thursday to cooperate more closely in preparing for membership.
"We agreed on a joint initiative for the future," Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus told a joint news conference with his Polish counterpart, Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz.
They said each government's foreign and defence ministries would set up consultations in areas of common interest.
"There are lots of questions which we can try to solve in consultations. The Poles and the Czechs are not competitiors. It's the other way. We can help each other with this," Cimoszewicz said.

While Poland has forged similar ties with Hungary, which is also seen as a prime prospect for NATO and EU membership, the Czechs have been reluctant to be seen as lumped with neighbours in upcoming accession talks.

NATO is expected to begin talks with potential new members after a summit this summer, while the EU has said it would open talks with former Soviet Bloc states about six months after the end of its ongoing government review process this year.
Klaus rejected that the Czechs had taken a lone wolf approach to joining the Western institutions, a charge often made privately by diplomats and politicians.
Neither would elaborate on specifically what form the cooperation would take, but Cimoszewicz listed modernisation of military equipment as one key area.
"Both countries need to modernise their armed forces which means it would be proper and wise to cooperate in this area," the Polish prime minister said.
Poland, the Czech Republic, and Hungary are all considering how to upgrade their armies, especially their air forces, with advanced equipment.
All three are searching for ways to augment ageing fleets of Soviet-made MiG fighter jets with "NATO-compatible" equipment, possibly U.S.-made fighters or those from European makers.

Both Klaus and Cimoszewicz said it was necessary to continue a dialogue with Russia, which is vehemently opposed to NATO's eastward expansion, but repeated that Moscow should not dictate decisions on NATO expansion.
